facts.claim: The Athenians defeated the Persians at Marathon
facts.context: A heavily outnumbered Athenian force beat the invading Persians in 490 BC.
facts.goDeeper: The modern marathon distance comes from the legend of a runner carrying news to Athens, a story no contemporary source records.

facts.claim: Leonidas and his Spartans held the pass at Thermopylae
facts.context: A Greek force delayed the Persian army for three days in 480 BC before being outflanked.
facts.goDeeper: The 300 Spartans were not alone; several thousand other Greeks fought there, and around 1,100 stayed to the end.

facts.claim: The Greek fleet destroyed the Persian navy at Salamis
facts.context: Fought weeks after Thermopylae, in the narrow straits near Athens.
facts.goDeeper: Themistocles had persuaded Athens to spend a silver windfall on warships instead of dividing it among citizens.

facts.claim: The first recorded Olympic Games were held at Olympia
facts.context: Traditionally dated to 776 BC and held every four years thereafter.
facts.goDeeper: The Games ran for roughly 1,200 years before a Roman emperor suppressed them as a pagan festival.

facts.claim: The Parthenon was completed on the Athenian Acropolis
facts.context: Construction ran from 447 to about 432 BC, during the height of Athenian power.
facts.goDeeper: It survived largely intact for over 2,000 years until 1687, when a Venetian shell hit the gunpowder stored inside.

facts.claim: The Peloponnesian War between Athens and Sparta began
facts.context: A 27-year conflict that ended with Athens defeated and stripped of its empire.
facts.goDeeper: Thucydides, who fought in it and was exiled for losing a command, wrote the history that still defines it.

facts.claim: Socrates was executed in Athens
facts.context: Condemned for impiety and corrupting the young, and made to drink hemlock.
facts.goDeeper: He wrote nothing. Everything we have comes through his students, chiefly Plato.

facts.claim: Cleisthenes established the reforms that founded Athenian democracy
facts.context: His reforms of 508-507 BC reorganised Athens around citizen assemblies rather than noble families.
facts.goDeeper: Citizenship excluded women, enslaved people and foreigners, so perhaps 10 to 20 percent of residents could vote.

facts.claim: Alexander the Great died in Babylon
facts.context: He died at 32, having conquered from Greece to the Indus in about a decade.
facts.goDeeper: His empire was carved up by his generals within a few years of his death.

facts.claim: Rome sacked Corinth, ending Greek independence
facts.context: The destruction of Corinth in 146 BC brought Greece firmly under Roman control.
facts.goDeeper: The Romans absorbed Greek art, religion and philosophy so thoroughly that Horace said captive Greece took Rome captive.

facts.claim: Number of independent Greek city-states at their height
facts.context: Around a thousand poleis are known across the Greek world, most of them tiny.
facts.goDeeper: They shared a language and gods but fought each other constantly. Unity came only under outside conquest.

facts.claim: Columns along the long side of the Parthenon
facts.context: Seventeen along each flank and eight across each end.
facts.goDeeper: Almost no line in the building is truly straight; the columns bulge and lean inward to correct for how the eye sees them.

facts.claim: Estimated population of Athens at its fifth-century peak
facts.context: Perhaps 250,000 to 300,000 in Athens and Attica, of whom around 30,000 to 40,000 were voting citizens.
facts.goDeeper: A large share of the population was enslaved, and the silver mines that funded the fleet were worked by them.

facts.claim: Capacity of the theatre at Epidaurus
facts.context: About 14,000 seats, built in the fourth century BC and still used today.
facts.goDeeper: Its acoustics are famous: a coin dropped on the stage floor can be heard from the back row.

facts.claim: Married women were barred from watching the ancient Olympics
facts.context: Married women were forbidden to attend the games at Olympia, on pain of death by some accounts.
facts.goDeeper: Women could nonetheless win the chariot race as owners of the team. Cynisca of Sparta did so twice.

facts.claim: Greek marble statues were originally left plain white
facts.context: They were painted in strong colours. Traces of pigment survive and can be revealed under ultraviolet light.
facts.goDeeper: The white ideal comes from Renaissance and 18th-century taste, looking at statues whose paint had long since weathered off.

facts.claim: Spartan boys were taken from their families for military training
facts.context: The agoge began at about age seven and continued into adulthood.
facts.goDeeper: Sparta was unusual in educating girls physically too, on the reasoning that strong mothers bore strong sons.

facts.claim: The Greeks built a geared mechanical device for predicting astronomical events
facts.context: The Antikythera mechanism, recovered from a shipwreck in 1901, used dozens of bronze gears to track the sun, moon and planets.
facts.goDeeper: Nothing of comparable mechanical complexity is known again for over a thousand years.

facts.claim: Greek scholars knew the Earth was a sphere and measured its size
facts.context: Eratosthenes calculated the Earth's circumference in the third century BC, within a few percent of the true figure.
facts.goDeeper: He did it using shadows at noon in two Egyptian cities and some careful geometry.

facts.claim: The Greek alphabet was the first to write vowels as separate letters
facts.context: Adapted from Phoenician, which wrote only consonants, with unused signs repurposed for vowel sounds.
facts.goDeeper: Every European alphabet in use today descends from that adaptation.
